title: Motor biases in visual attention for a humanoid robot

fields.value: Technical/system description with preliminary experiments on a humanoid robot.

quotes.text: In this paper we aim at implementing these features to control attention in a humanoid robot by including a set of trajectory predictors in the simple but effective form of Kalman filters, and, more importantly, a reinforcement learning based process that utilizes the predictors and the complete set of actions of the robot repertoire to generate a suitably optimal action sequence.

Preliminary experiments show that the system indeed works correctly: it uses the predictors to discriminate the environmental context (e.g. static vs. dynamic) and produces a valid control policy that drives the robot to fixation of the task- relevant static or moving stimuli.

fields.value: The authors state that the humanoid platform is suitable for studying visual attention in human–robot interaction and that foveated vision requires eye movements to acquire a high-resolution internal image. No effect of embodiment on the study outcomes is reported.

quotes.text: Our experimental platform is the iCub [15], a full-fledged humanoid robot sporting among other things independently movable eyes neck, visual inertial sensors, and facial features, which therefore make it an ideal platform for the study of visual attention during human-robot interaction.
Differently from Itti Koch’s model, the use of foveated vision requires the robot to move the eyes in order to acquire a high-resolution internal image of the visual scene [18].

fields.value: The paper implements visual attention and learned gaze control on the iCub humanoid, using saliency, trajectory prediction, and reinforcement learning. In tabletop experiments with static objects and a human-moved ball, learning produced policies that brought the robot to fixation and reduced actions or trajectory duration; it did not study multiparty interaction effects.

RQ1; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper describes attention as ocular movement toward an attended location, details its autonomous prediction and learning implementation, and describes the iCub embodiment and its eye movement requirements. It does not investigate multiparty interaction or its effects on people.
